noqa: BLE001\n             return _error_response(buffered, error)\n \n","issue":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\"id\":\"AUTH-1\",\"title\":\"Support canonical-gateway routing in AuthFn multi-region\",\"description\":\"## Executive summary\\n\\nExtend AuthFn's existing multi-region plugin so applications can expose one canonical public authority while a trusted gateway resolves and dispatches authentication requests to the owning regional cell. In gateway mode, browsers, mobile clients, and MCP/OAuth clients continue to use the canonical hostname; regional authorities remain an optional direct-routing deployment mode, not a client requirement.\\n\\nThe implementation must remain provider-neutral. A consumer may back the global identity-to-region directory with DynamoDB Global Tables, Cloudflare Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or another adapter that satisfies AuthFn's consistency contract.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `authfn/multi-region/src/index.ts` registers `beforeUserCreate`, `afterUserCreate`, `beforeSessionIssue`, and `afterAccountDelete` hooks and exposes `POST /regions/lookup` plus `GET /environment`.\\n* `authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts` resolves the current region primarily from request host/authority, performs lookup/registration through `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, and raises `AuthFnRegionMismatchError` for the client to follow.\\n* `authfn/client/src/regional-client.ts` keeps a local identifier-to-region cache and requires `resolveBaseUrl(regionId)`; routing retries therefore live in every client.\\n* `authfn/core/src/plugin-types.ts` already defines region, lookup, registration, and runtime configuration contracts.\\n* `packages/db/src/adapter/types.ts` provides atomic `setIfAbsent` and optional `compareAndSet`.\\n* Python's `authfn/plugins/multi_region.py` uses a separate duck-typed `directory.lookup_by_identifier/register_user` contract and does not currently expose the same atomic ownership semantics as TypeScript.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nThe existing model assumes the caller can discover a user's region, map a region ID to a public hostname, and retry against that hostname. That complicates every client and OAuth callback, exposes deployment topology, and makes canonical issuer/cookie behavior harder to reason about.\\n\\nMoving this logic to a gateway creates a shared dependency: if the global ingress or directory cannot route a request, otherwise healthy regional authentication cells may be unreachable through the canonical authority. The contract must therefore define availability, caching, consistency, and failure behavior explicitly rather than hiding them inside one provider integration.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Add a gateway-routed mode while preserving the current direct regional-authority mode.\\n* Keep one stable public issuer/base URL for browser auth, OAuth discovery/callbacks, MCP authorization, and native handoff flows.\\n* Make regional lookup and dispatch a server-side concern; clients do not need regional DNS names or `resolveBaseUrl` in gateway mode.\\n* Keep lookup storage and inter-region transport provider-neutral.\\n* Preserve atomic, deterministic account placement under concurrent sign-up.\\n* Avoid turning the public lookup endpoint into an account-enumeration or topology-disclosure surface.\\n* Bring TypeScript and Python behavior and interfaces into parity.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Separate public authority from execution region\\n\\nIntroduce explicit concepts for:\\n\\n* canonical public authority/issuer;\\n* current execution `regionId`;\\n* internal regional destination;\\n* routing mode (`direct` or `gateway`);\\n* routing version/epoch used to reject stale decisions.\\n\\nHost matching may remain for direct mode, but gateway mode must not infer ownership from the public host because every request arrives on the same hostname.\\n\\n### 2. Define a gateway-facing routing contract\\n\\nProvide a framework-owned contract that a gateway can call before invoking AuthFn, for example a resolver/dispatcher result containing:\\n\\n* normalized lookup key or opaque routing subject;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* routing epoch/version;\\n* decision status (`local`, `forward`, `unknown`, `moving`, `unavailable`);\\n* an internal destination token or adapter-owned handle, not necessarily a public URL;\\n* cacheability/expiry metadata.\\n\\nDo not require Cloudflare Service Bindings, DynamoDB, or any specific transport in the core API. Provider packages may adapt the contract.\\n\\n### 3. Keep placement atomic\\n\\nContinue to use `setIfAbsent` for first ownership and use `compareAndSet` (or an equivalent required capability) for controlled moves. Specify normalized identifier keys, conflict handling, deletion/tombstone behavior, read consistency, and replication-lag expectations.\\n\\nAn account must never be created in two regions when concurrent requests race. Registration rollback and retry behavior must be tested under partial failure.\\n\\n### 4. Add trusted internal forwarding\\n\\nDefine a short-lived signed internal routing assertion containing at least request ID, target region, routing epoch, issued/expiry timestamps, and a replay-resistant nonce or equivalent transport protection. Regional handlers must reject user-supplied forwarding headers and validate the assertion before trusting gateway routing context.\\n\\nForwarding must preserve method, path, body, cookies, CSRF properties, client IP provenance policy, and request correlation without leaking internal destinations to callers.\\n\\n### 5. Make retries side-effect safe\\n\\nA regional instance must validate placement before creating users, issuing sessions/codes/tokens, sending OTP email, or performing any other externally visible effect. If the decision is stale, return a machine-readable internal mismatch response and let the gateway re-resolve and retry at most once.\\n\\nDo not automatically replay requests after a side effect may have occurred. Define idempotency requirements for OTP send, OAuth authorization/token exchange, account creation, API-key operations, password reset, email change, native handoff, and deletion.\\n\\n### 6. Preserve canonical OAuth/session semantics\\n\\nIn gateway mode:\\n\\n* OAuth metadata, authorization endpoint, token endpoint, redirect URIs, and issuer remain canonical.\\n* OAuth state/authorization requests/codes and native handoff artifacts carry enough region/epoch context to return to the correct cell without changing the browser-visible host.\\n* Cookies retain one documented domain/name/security policy across regions.\\n* Sessions expose region metadata only where useful and do not require a regional public origin.\\n* Logout, revocation, refresh rotation, account deletion, and session invalidation work across the canonical authority.\\n\\n### 7. Harden public behavior\\n\\nThe public API must not reveal whether an identifier exists, its user ID, its region, or internal authority unless a consumer explicitly opts into the legacy/direct lookup behavior and accepts that security posture. Gateway lookup should be an authenticated internal capability.\\n\\nUpdate event/metric schemas to distinguish lookup hit/miss/conflict, forwarding, stale epoch, retry, directory unavailable, and target unavailable without logging raw identifiers.\\n\\n### 8. TypeScript/Python parity and compatibility\\n\\nDefine one documented semantic contract across both SDKs. Existing direct-mode configuration and regional client behavior remain backward compatible. Add migration notes for consumers moving from public regional authorities to a canonical gateway.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n- [ ] A client configured only with a canonical AuthFn base URL can complete OTP sign-up/sign-in, cookie sessions, OAuth authorization-code + refresh, API-key auth, logout/revocation, and native handoff for users owned by at least two regions.\\n- [ ] The gateway resolves and forwards without returning a regional hostname to the client.\\n- [ ] Direct regional-authority mode and existing `resolveBaseUrl` clients continue to work.\\n- [ ] Concurrent first sign-up claims cannot create the same normalized identifier in two regions.\\n- [ ] Stale routing produces a pre-side-effect mismatch, one bounded gateway re-resolution, and no duplicate In gateway mode, browsers, mobile clients, and MCP/OAuth clients continue to use the canonical hostname; regional authorities remain an optional direct-routing deployment mode, not a client requirement.\\n\\nThe implementation must remain provider-neutral. A consumer may back the global identity-to-region directory with DynamoDB Global Tables, Cloudflare Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or another adapter that satisfies AuthFn's consistency contract.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `authfn/multi-region/src/index.ts` registers `beforeUserCreate`, `afterUserCreate`, `beforeSessionIssue`, and `afterAccountDelete` hooks and exposes `POST /regions/lookup` plus `GET /environment`.\\n* `authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts` resolves the current region primarily from request host/authority, performs lookup/registration through `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, and raises `AuthFnRegionMismatchError` for the client to follow.\\n* `authfn/client/src/regional-client.ts` keeps a local identifier-to-region cache and requires `resolveBaseUrl(regionId)`; routing retries therefore live in every client.\\n* `authfn/core/src/plugin-types.ts` already defines region, lookup, registration, and runtime configuration contracts.\\n* `packages/db/src/adapter/types.ts` provides atomic `setIfAbsent` and optional `compareAndSet`.\\n* Python's `authfn/plugins/multi_region.py` uses a separate duck-typed `directory.lookup_by_identifier/register_user` contract and does not currently expose the same atomic ownership semantics as TypeScript.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nThe existing model assumes the caller can discover a user's region, map a region ID to a public hostname, and retry against that hostname. That complicates every client and OAuth callback, exposes deployment topology, and makes canonical issuer/cookie behavior harder to reason about.\\n\\nMoving this logic to a gateway creates a shared dependency: if the global ingress or directory cannot route a request, otherwise healthy regional authentication cells may be unreachable through the canonical authority. The contract must therefore define availability, caching, consistency, and failure behavior explicitly rather than hiding them inside one provider integration.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Add a gateway-routed mode while preserving the current direct regional-authority mode.\\n* Keep one stable public issuer/base URL for browser auth, OAuth discovery/callbacks, MCP authorization, and native handoff flows.\\n* Make regional lookup and dispatch a server-side concern; clients do not need regional DNS names or `resolveBaseUrl` in gateway mode.\\n* Keep lookup storage and inter-region transport provider-neutral.\\n* Preserve atomic, deterministic account placement under concurrent sign-up.\\n* Avoid turning the public lookup endpoint into an account-enumeration or topology-disclosure surface.\\n* Bring TypeScript and Python behavior and interfaces into parity.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Separate public authority from execution region\\n\\nIntroduce explicit concepts for:\\n\\n* canonical public authority/issuer;\\n* current execution `regionId`;\\n* internal regional destination;\\n* routing mode (`direct` or `gateway`);\\n* routing version/epoch used to reject stale decisions.\\n\\nHost matching may remain for direct mode, but gateway mode must not infer ownership from the public host because every request arrives on the same hostname.\\n\\n### 2. Define a gateway-facing routing contract\\n\\nProvide a framework-owned contract that a gateway can call before invoking AuthFn, for example a resolver/dispatcher result containing:\\n\\n* normalized lookup key or opaque routing subject;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* routing epoch/version;\\n* decision status (`local`, `forward`, `unknown`, `moving`, `unavailable`);\\n* an internal destination token or adapter-owned handle, not necessarily a public URL;\\n* cacheability/expiry metadata.\\n\\nDo not require Cloudflare Service Bindings, DynamoDB, or any specific transport in the core API. Provider packages may adapt the contract.\\n\\n### 3. Keep placement atomic\\n\\nContinue to use `setIfAbsent` for first ownership and use `compareAndSet` (or an equivalent required capability) for controlled moves. Specify normalized identifier keys, conflict handling, deletion/tombstone behavior, read consistency, and replication-lag expectations.\\n\\nAn account must never be created in two regions when concurrent requests race. Registration rollback and retry behavior must be tested under partial failure.\\n\\n### 4. Add trusted internal forwarding\\n\\nDefine a short-lived signed internal routing assertion containing at least request ID, target region, routing epoch, issued/expiry timestamps, and a replay-resistant nonce or equivalent transport protection. Make retries side-effect safe\\n\\nA regional instance must validate placement before creating users, issuing sessions/codes/tokens, sending OTP email, or performing any other externally visible effect. If the decision is stale, return a machine-readable internal mismatch response and let the gateway re-resolve and retry at most once.\\n\\nDo not automatically replay requests after a side effect may have occurred. Define idempotency requirements for OTP send, OAuth authorization/token exchange, account creation, API-key operations, password reset, email change, native handoff, and deletion.\\n\\n### 6. email/session/code/token side effects.\\n- [ ] Missing directory or target-cell availability fails with explicit retryable/non-retryable errors and documented cache/fail-closed behavior.\\n- [ ] Applications should be able to expose one stable DataFn endpoint while a trusted gateway resolves a namespace/tenant to its owning regional cell and dispatches the request server-side.\\n\\nThe core contract must remain provider-neutral and must not require clients to resolve regional hostnames.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `datafn/server/src/plugins/multi-region.ts` defines `datafnMultiRegionPlugin({ regionId, directory })`, but the directory currently indexes permission grants only.\\n* The existing index records `resourceRegion` and supports principal/resource queries through `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter`.\\n* Permission-directory writes already use a durable post-commit outbox/retry path under `datafn/server/src/execution/mutation/permission-directory-outbox.ts`.\\n* `datafn/server/src/server.ts` builds one server around one database adapter. Request context and `namespaceProvider` select a namespace, but no first-class hook validates that the namespace belongs to the current regional database or dispatches to another server.\\n* `datafn/core/src/types.ts` exposes query/search/mutation/sync hooks, but no region-placement, pre-execution routing, or transport-forwarding contract.\\n* `datafn/client/src/transport/http.ts` uses a fixed base URL and only retries authorization failures; `datafn/client/src/client.ts` accepts a fixed `remote` or custom `remoteAdapter`.\\n* `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter` offers indexed reads and `putIfAbsent`, but `update` is not compare-and-set; `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter` separately exposes optional `compareAndSet`.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nDataFn can tell consumers that a shared resource grant originated in a region, but it cannot authoritatively place a tenant namespace, reject execution in the wrong regional database, or let a global gateway forward a request safely. Applications would otherwise need to build their own router around DataFn and teach clients about regional endpoints, fragmenting behavior across consumers.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Make tenant/namespace placement a first-class DataFn multi-region capability.\\n* Support a canonical gateway URL with no regional hostname resolution in clients.\\n* Preserve current single-region and permission-directory behavior.\\n* Keep storage and transport adapters cloud/provider neutral.\\n* Guarantee that wrong-region detection happens before reads/writes are executed.\\n* Cover HTTP query/mutation/search, sync/push/pull/reconcile, in-process execution, and WebSocket lifecycle.\\n* Define safe placement changes without claiming transparent active-active writes.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Distinguish placement from permission indexing\\n\\nExtend or compose `datafnMultiRegionPlugin` with an authoritative placement directory. A placement record should include at least:\\n\\n* stable tenant/namespace ID;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* monotonically changing routing epoch/version;\\n* lifecycle state (`active`, `moving`, `tombstoned`);\\n* updated timestamp and optional cache expiry;\\n* adapter-owned internal destination reference, separate from a public URL.\\n\\nPermission-grant indexing may reference placement, but it must not become the source of truth for namespace ownership. Document separate consistency and recovery guarantees for both directories.\\n\\n### 2. Define provider-neutral directory capabilities\\n\\nSpecify the atomic contract needed for initial `putIfAbsent` placement and controlled compare-and-set moves. Decide whether to extend `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter`, compose it with `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, or introduce a focused `DatafnPlacementDirectoryAdapter`.\\n\\nCore must run against in-memory/test adapters. Provider integrations may implement DynamoDB Global Tables, Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or other stores.\\n\\n### 3. Add pre-execution placement validation\\n\\nResolve the trusted namespace after authentication/context construction and before authorization side effects, database queries, mutations, sync changes, or plugin hooks that assume local ownership.\\n\\nIf the current server does not own the namespace/epoch, return a typed internal `DATAFN_REGION_MISMATCH`/moving response containing safe routing metadata. Do not trust a raw client-supplied namespace or region header without existing authentication and namespace authorization.\\n\\nThis validation must also cover in-process executor requests and custom server routes that operate on regional data.\\n\\n### 4. Add a gateway dispatcher/transport contract\\n\\nProvide an adapter boundary that lets a canonical ingress:\\n\\n1. authenticate enough context to derive the tenant/namespace;\\n2. resolve placement;\\n3. forward internally to the owning cell;\\n4. attach a short-lived signed routing assertion;\\n5. retry one time after a pre-execution stale-epoch response.\\n\\nThe internal destination may be a service binding, HTTP origin, RPC stub, or function reference. DataFn core must not depend on Cloudflare, AWS, DNS, or public regional URLs.\\n\\n### 5. Preserve request semantics and idempotency\\n\\nForward method, path, body, auth context, request/correlation ID, namespace, and idempotency identity without allowing callers to forge gateway headers. Define bounded retry rules for:\\n\\n* query/search/status;\\n* mutation/transact;\\n* push/pull/reconcile/seed/clone;\\n* public-link and permission-grant operations;\\n* custom plugin routes.\\n\\nMutating replay is allowed only when DataFn can prove the original request did not begin execution or when the operation's existing idempotency key makes replay safe.\\n\\n### 6. Define WebSocket and sync behavior\\n\\nA WebSocket/sync session is routed during handshake and pinned to namespace + region + routing epoch. When placement changes, the old cell must stop accepting new work and cause clients to reconnect through the canonical gateway. Ordering, cursor semantics, mutation IDs, and pull checkpoints must remain valid or fail explicitly across migration.\\n\\nThe browser/client API should continue to accept one stable `remote`/`wsUrl` in gateway mode. Direct regional routing can remain an opt-in adapter mode.\\n\\n### 7. Placement migration protocol\\n\\nDocument and implement a minimal safe state machine, including:\\n\\n* quiesce/fence source writes;\\n* drain/reconcile outbox work;\\n* copy and validate tenant data;\\n* atomically advance the placement epoch;\\n* warm/route target reads;\\n* resume writes;\\n* retain rollback/tombstone evidence.\\n\\nNo request may write to both cells because of stale cache state. State transitions and failure recovery must be observable and testable.\\n\\n### 8. Observability and compatibility\\n\\nEmit safe events/metrics for placement lookup, cache hit, forward, mismatch, retry, moving, directory unavailable, destination unavailable, and epoch conflict. Existing single-region configurations and the current permission-directory API must remain source-compatible.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n- [ ] A DataFn client configured with one canonical HTTP endpoint can query and mutate namespaces owned by at least two regional database adapters without learning regional hostnames.\\n- [ ] Current single-region servers and permission-directory grant indexing continue to pass their existing tests.\\n- [ ] Every built-in HTTP, sync, in-process, and WebSocket entry path validates placement before regional database execution.\\n- [ ] A caller cannot route into or select another tenant by spoofing namespace, region, epoch, or internal-forwarding headers.\\n- [ ] Initial placement is atomic, and placement moves use a fenced compare-and-set epoch transition.\\n- [ ] Stale gateway cache causes at most one bounded re-resolution/retry and no duplicate mutation side effects.\\n- [ ] WebSocket clients reconnect through the canonical gateway on a move, with explicit cursor/checkpoint behavior.\\n- [ ] Permission-directory outbox behavior is reconciled with placement moves; failed indexing does not silently change ownership.\\n- [ ] Directory and target-cell outages return documented retryability and do not route to a random/default region.\\n- [ ] Core conformance tests run with in-memory adapters, and at least two provider adapters demonstrate portability.\\n- [ ] Public API/type documentation explains gateway mode, direct mode, consistency, migration, and operational requirements.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n\\n* Implementing a Skillplane-specific workspace directory.\\n* Requiring active-active writes for the same namespace.\\n* Choosing a cloud provider, global database, DNS layout, or edge platform.\\n* Automatically moving a tenant solely because a regional health check fails.\",\"priority\":{\"value\":0,\"name\":\"No In gateway mode, browsers, mobile clients, and MCP/OAuth clients continue to use the canonical hostname; regional authorities remain an optional direct-routing deployment mode, not a client requirement.\\n\\nThe implementation must remain provider-neutral. A consumer may back the global identity-to-region directory with DynamoDB Global Tables, Cloudflare Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or another adapter that satisfies AuthFn's consistency contract.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `authfn/multi-region/src/index.ts` registers `beforeUserCreate`, `afterUserCreate`, `beforeSessionIssue`, and `afterAccountDelete` hooks and exposes `POST /regions/lookup` plus `GET /environment`.\\n* `authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts` resolves the current region primarily from request host/authority, performs lookup/registration through `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, and raises `AuthFnRegionMismatchError` for the client to follow.\\n* `authfn/client/src/regional-client.ts` keeps a local identifier-to-region cache and requires `resolveBaseUrl(regionId)`; routing retries therefore live in every client.\\n* `authfn/core/src/plugin-types.ts` already defines region, lookup, registration, and runtime configuration contracts.\\n* `packages/db/src/adapter/types.ts` provides atomic `setIfAbsent` and optional `compareAndSet`.\\n* Python's `authfn/plugins/multi_region.py` uses a separate duck-typed `directory.lookup_by_identifier/register_user` contract and does not currently expose the same atomic ownership semantics as TypeScript.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nThe existing model assumes the caller can discover a user's region, map a region ID to a public hostname, and retry against that hostname. That complicates every client and OAuth callback, exposes deployment topology, and makes canonical issuer/cookie behavior harder to reason about.\\n\\nMoving this logic to a gateway creates a shared dependency: if the global ingress or directory cannot route a request, otherwise healthy regional authentication cells may be unreachable through the canonical authority. The contract must therefore define availability, caching, consistency, and failure behavior explicitly rather than hiding them inside one provider integration.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Add a gateway-routed mode while preserving the current direct regional-authority mode.\\n* Keep one stable public issuer/base URL for browser auth, OAuth discovery/callbacks, MCP authorization, and native handoff flows.\\n* Make regional lookup and dispatch a server-side concern; clients do not need regional DNS names or `resolveBaseUrl` in gateway mode.\\n* Keep lookup storage and inter-region transport provider-neutral.\\n* Preserve atomic, deterministic account placement under concurrent sign-up.\\n* Avoid turning the public lookup endpoint into an account-enumeration or topology-disclosure surface.\\n* Bring TypeScript and Python behavior and interfaces into parity.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Separate public authority from execution region\\n\\nIntroduce explicit concepts for:\\n\\n* canonical public authority/issuer;\\n* current execution `regionId`;\\n* internal regional destination;\\n* routing mode (`direct` or `gateway`);\\n* routing version/epoch used to reject stale decisions.\\n\\nHost matching may remain for direct mode, but gateway mode must not infer ownership from the public host because every request arrives on the same hostname.\\n\\n### 2. Define a gateway-facing routing contract\\n\\nProvide a framework-owned contract that a gateway can call before invoking AuthFn, for example a resolver/dispatcher result containing:\\n\\n* normalized lookup key or opaque routing subject;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* routing epoch/version;\\n* decision status (`local`, `forward`, `unknown`, `moving`, `unavailable`);\\n* an internal destination token or adapter-owned handle, not necessarily a public URL;\\n* cacheability/expiry metadata.\\n\\nDo not require Cloudflare Service Bindings, DynamoDB, or any specific transport in the core API. Provider packages may adapt the contract.\\n\\n### 3. Keep placement atomic\\n\\nContinue to use `setIfAbsent` for first ownership and use `compareAndSet` (or an equivalent required capability) for controlled moves. Specify normalized identifier keys, conflict handling, deletion/tombstone behavior, read consistency, and replication-lag expectations.\\n\\nAn account must never be created in two regions when concurrent requests race. Registration rollback and retry behavior must be tested under partial failure.\\n\\n### 4. Add trusted internal forwarding\\n\\nDefine a short-lived signed internal routing assertion containing at least request ID, target region, routing epoch, issued/expiry timestamps, and a replay-resistant nonce or equivalent transport protection. Regional handlers must reject user-supplied forwarding headers and validate the assertion before trusting gateway routing context.\\n\\nForwarding must preserve method, path, body, cookies, CSRF properties, client IP provenance policy, and request correlation without leaking internal destinations to callers.\\n\\n### 5. Make retries side-effect safe\\n\\nA regional instance must validate placement before creating users, issuing sessions/codes/tokens, sending OTP email, or performing any other externally visible effect. If the decision is stale, return a machine-readable internal mismatch response and let the gateway re-resolve and retry at most once.\\n\\nDo not automatically replay requests after a side effect may have occurred. Define idempotency requirements for OTP send, OAuth authorization/token exchange, account creation, API-key operations, password reset, email change, native handoff, and deletion.\\n\\n### 6. Preserve canonical OAuth/session semantics\\n\\nIn gateway mode:\\n\\n* OAuth metadata, authorization endpoint, token endpoint, redirect URIs, and issuer remain canonical.\\n* OAuth state/authorization requests/codes and native handoff artifacts carry enough region/epoch context to return to the correct cell without changing the browser-visible host.\\n* Cookies retain one documented domain/name/security policy across regions.\\n* Sessions expose region metadata only where useful and do not require a regional public origin.\\n* Logout, revocation, refresh rotation, account deletion, and session invalidation work across the canonical authority.\\n\\n### 7. Harden public behavior\\n\\nThe public API must not reveal whether an identifier exists, its user ID, its region, or internal authority unless a consumer explicitly opts into the legacy/direct lookup behavior and accepts that security posture. Gateway lookup should be an authenticated internal capability.\\n\\nUpdate event/metric schemas to distinguish lookup hit/miss/conflict, forwarding, stale epoch, retry, directory unavailable, and target unavailable without logging raw identifiers.\\n\\n### 8. TypeScript/Python parity and compatibility\\n\\nDefine one documented semantic contract across both SDKs. Existing direct-mode configuration and regional client behavior remain backward compatible. Add migration notes for consumers moving from public regional authorities to a canonical gateway.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n- [ ] A client configured only with a canonical AuthFn base URL can complete OTP sign-up/sign-in, cookie sessions, OAuth authorization-code + refresh, API-key auth, logout/revocation, and native handoff for users owned by at least two regions.\\n- [ ] The gateway resolves and forwards without returning a regional hostname to the client.\\n- [ ] Direct regional-authority mode and existing `resolveBaseUrl` clients continue to work.\\n- [ ] Concurrent first sign-up claims cannot create the same normalized identifier in two regions.\\n- [ ] Stale routing produces a pre-side-effect mismatch, one bounded gateway re-resolution, and no duplicate email/session/code/token side effects.\\n- [ ] Missing directory or target-cell availability fails with explicit retryable/non-retryable errors and documented cache/fail-closed behavior.\\n- [ ] User-controlled headers cannot spoof region, epoch, or internal forwarding identity.\\n- [ ] Public responses do not disclose account existence or regional topology in gateway mode.\\n- [ ] OAuth issuer/resource discovery and callback URLs remain canonical throughout the flow.\\n- [ ] TypeScript and Python conformance suites cover equivalent lookup, claim, mismatch, routing, and failure semantics.\\n- [ ] Core tests use in-memory adapters; at least two provider adapters demonstrate the same conformance contract without becoming core dependencies.\\n- [ ] Architecture and migration documentation explain the global dependency and operational SLOs.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n\\n* Building Skillplane's deployment topology in AuthFn.\\n* Mandating active-active writes for one account.\\n* Requiring a particular cloud, DNS provider, global database, or service-binding product.\\n* Silently failing over an account to another region without an explicit migration Work an Existing Linear Issue\n\nTreat the master as the user or orchestrating agent that supplied the Linear issue and controls publication approval.\n\n## Preconditions\n\n- Require an exact Linear issue identifier or URL from the master.\n- Require access to the Linear workspace and the relevant repository.\n- If the issue, repository, or authorization cannot be resolved exactly, stop and ask the master. Never guess.\n- Do not create a branch, commit, push, or pull request before the approval gate below.\n\n## 1. Read the complete Linear record\n\nUse the connected Linear tools as the authoritative issue source.\n\n1. Retrieve the issue by its exact identifier with relations and releases when supported.\n2. Read the full description, acceptance criteria, status, priority, labels, assignee, project, cycle, parent, sub-issues, blockers, blocked items, related issues, releases, links, and attachments.\n3. Read every issue comment and continue through pagination until complete.\n4. Follow linked Linear documents or projects when they contain requirements needed to execute the issue.\n5. Inspect embedded images or attachments when they may contain requirements or reproduction evidence.\n6. Distinguish explicit requirements from discussion, inference, and superseded guidance. Prefer the newest explicit decision when comments revise the description.\n7. Record the issue identifier exactly as Linear displays it; this exact value will become the branch name after approval.\n\nDo not begin implementation from a search snippet, truncated summary, issue title alone, or second-hand paraphrase.\n\n## 2. Establish repository scope\n\n- Resolve the target repository and its default branch from the issue, repository metadata, linked pull requests, or the master.\n- Inspect repository instructions, contribution rules, relevant specifications, tests, and surrounding implementation before editing.\n- Inspect Git status first. Preserve all pre-existing changes and never include unrelated work.\n- If the checkout has overlapping user changes, is based on an ambiguous branch, or does not match the issue's repository, stop and ask the master before modifying it.\n- Do not fetch, switch branches, rewrite history, discard changes, or publish anything merely to resolve ambiguity.\n\n## 3. Clarify only when needed\n\nAfter reading the entire issue and inspecting the relevant code, identify missing decisions that would materially change the implementation, acceptance criteria, security, data handling, compatibility, deployment behavior, or public API.\n\n- Ask the master concise, specific questions for blocking ambiguities.\n- Explain the competing interpretations and their impact.\n- Pause until answered when a reasonable assumption could produce the wrong product behavior or an unsafe change.\n- If no blocking ambiguity remains, state any low-risk assumptions and continue without asking ceremonial questions.\n- Treat answers from the master as additions to the issue requirements. Re-read the issue if the master says it was updated.\n\n## 4. Implement and verify locally\n\n- Implement only the issue scope, including required tests, documentation, migrations, or generated artifacts.\n- Follow repository-native patterns and use the narrowest non-regressive change.\n- Preserve unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked files.\n- Validate in proportion to risk. Run focused tests first, then the broader required gates.\n- Diagnose failures and distinguish issue-caused failures from pre-existing or environmental failures.\n- Do not claim completion while acceptance criteria remain unverified.\n- Do not create a branch, commit, push, pull request, release, or deployment during this stage unless the master separately expands the scope.\n\n## Linear comment hygiene\n\nBefore creating or updating a Linear comment, re-read the issue's existing comments and locate the latest comment created by this agent for the current work cycle.\n\n- Maintain one canonical completion and publication comment.\n- Retain the canonical comment ID so the same comment can be updated after publication.\n- Treat a proposed comment as a near duplicate when it repeats the same implementation summary, design decisions, verification results, and risks while only adding branch, commit, push, or pull-request metadata.\n- Update the canonical comment instead of creating a near duplicate.\n- Skip the write entirely when it adds no new information.\n- Add a follow-up comment only for a material delta, such as changed requirements, additional fixes, new verification results, a blocker or its resolution, or a new rollout or review decision.\n- Keep follow-up comments delta-only. Do not repeat unchanged implementation and verification summaries.\n- If comment updates are unavailable, post a short delta-only follow-up rather than another completion-style summary.\n\n## 5. Report completion on Linear\n\nWhen the implementation and local verification are complete, create or update one canonical comment on the original Linear issue containing:\n\n- What was implemented.\n- Important behavior or design decisions.\n- Files or system areas changed.\n- Tests and checks run, with pass/fail counts where available.\n- Any verification that could not be run and the exact reason.\n- Remaining risks, follow-ups, migrations, or rollout requirements.\n- A clear statement that the work is local and awaiting the master's approval for branch and pull-request publication.\n\nIf this agent already posted a canonical completion comment for the current work cycle, update that comment rather than creating another. Retain the returned comment ID for the publication update.\n\nDo not post a completion comment if required work is still incomplete. Post a blocker update instead when progress cannot continue.\n\nAfter commenting, summarize the same state to the master and explicitly request publication approval.\n\n## 6. Approval gate\n\nWait for an explicit approval from the master to publish.\n\nApproval must clearly authorize creating the issue branch and pull request for this completed work. Silence, issue assignment, a Linear status change, an earlier request to implement, or approval from another agent does not satisfy this gate.\n\nIf the master requests changes instead:\n\n1. Apply and verify them.\n2. Add a delta-only follow-up comment when the changes are material, covering only the new fixes, decisions, and verification. Otherwise update the canonical comment.\n3. Request approval again.\n\n## 7. Create the issue branch and pull request\n\nOnly after explicit approval:\n\n1. Re-read the Linear issue and its newest comments for late changes.\n2. Recheck repository status and confirm the repository default branch.\n3. Confirm the local change set contains only work for this issue.\n4. Create a new branch whose name is exactly the Linear issue identifier, for example `SKI-123`. Do not add a prefix or description.\n5. If that exact branch already exists locally or remotely, inspect it and ask the master before reusing, overwriting, renaming, or force-pushing it.\n6. Stage only issue-scoped files.\n7. Create an intentional commit referencing the Linear issue identifier.\n8. Push the new branch without force.\n9. Create a pull request into the repository's confirmed default branch.\n10. Treat the master as the user or orchestrating agent that supplied the Linear issue and controls publication approval.

## Preconditions

- Require an exact Linear issue identifier or URL from the master.
- Require access to the Linear workspace and the relevant repository.
- If the issue, repository, or authorization cannot be resolved exactly, stop and ask the master. Never guess.
- Do not create a branch, commit, push, or pull request before the approval gate below.

## 1. Read the complete Linear record

Use the connected Linear tools as the authoritative issue source.

1. Retrieve the issue by its exact identifier with relations and releases when supported.
2. Read the full description, acceptance criteria, status, priority, labels, assignee, project, cycle, parent, sub-issues, blockers, blocked items, related issues, releases, links, and attachments.
3. Read every issue comment and continue through pagination until complete.
4. Follow linked Linear documents or projects when they contain requirements needed to execute the issue.
5. Inspect embedded images or attachments when they may contain requirements or reproduction evidence.
6. Distinguish explicit requirements from discussion, inference, and superseded guidance. Prefer the newest explicit decision when comments revise the description.
7. Record the issue identifier exactly as Linear displays it; this exact value will become the branch name after approval.

Do not begin implementation from a search snippet, truncated summary, issue title alone, or second-hand paraphrase.

## 2. Establish repository scope

- Resolve the target repository and its default branch from the issue, repository metadata, linked pull requests, or the master.
- Inspect repository instructions, contribution rules, relevant specifications, tests, and surrounding implementation before editing.
- Inspect Git status first. Preserve all pre-existing changes and never include unrelated work.
- If the checkout has overlapping user changes, is based on an ambiguous branch, or does not match the issue's repository, stop and ask the master before modifying it.
- Do not fetch, switch branches, rewrite history, discard changes, or publish anything merely to resolve ambiguity.

## 3. Clarify only when needed

After reading the entire issue and inspecting the relevant code, identify missing decisions that would materially change the implementation, acceptance criteria, security, data handling, compatibility, deployment behavior, or public API.

- Ask the master concise, specific questions for blocking ambiguities.
- Explain the competing interpretations and their impact.
- Pause until answered when a reasonable assumption could produce the wrong product behavior or an unsafe change.
- If no blocking ambiguity remains, state any low-risk assumptions and continue without asking ceremonial questions.
- Treat answers from the master as additions to the issue requirements. Re-read the issue if the master says it was updated.

## 4. Implement and verify locally

- Implement only the issue scope, including required tests, documentation, migrations, or generated artifacts.
- Follow repository-native patterns and use the narrowest non-regressive change.
- Preserve unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked files.
- Validate in proportion to risk. Run focused tests first, then the broader required gates.
- Diagnose failures and distinguish issue-caused failures from pre-existing or environmental failures.
- Do not claim completion while acceptance criteria remain unverified.
- Do not create a branch, commit, push, pull request, release, or deployment during this stage unless the master separately expands the scope.

## Linear comment hygiene

Before creating or updating a Linear comment, re-read the issue's existing comments and locate the latest comment created by this agent for the current work cycle.

- Maintain one canonical completion and publication comment.
- Retain the canonical comment ID so the same comment can be updated after publication.
- Treat a proposed comment as a near duplicate when it repeats the same implementation summary, design decisions, verification results, and risks while only adding branch, commit, push, or pull-request metadata.
- Update the canonical comment instead of creating a near duplicate.
- Skip the write entirely when it adds no new information.
- Add a follow-up comment only for a material delta, such as changed requirements, additional fixes, new verification results, a blocker or its resolution, or a new rollout or review decision.
- Keep follow-up comments delta-only. Do not repeat unchanged implementation and verification summaries.
- If comment updates are unavailable, post a short delta-only follow-up rather than another completion-style summary.

## 5. Report completion on Linear

When the implementation and local verification are complete, create or update one canonical comment on the original Linear issue containing:

- What was implemented.
- Important behavior or design decisions.
- Files or system areas changed.
- Tests and checks run, with pass/fail counts where available.
- Any verification that could not be run and the exact reason.
- Remaining risks, follow-ups, migrations, or rollout requirements.
- A clear statement that the work is local and awaiting the master's approval for branch and pull-request publication.

If this agent already posted a canonical completion comment for the current work cycle, update that comment rather than creating another. Retain the returned comment ID for the publication update.

Do not post a completion comment if required work is still incomplete. Post a blocker update instead when progress cannot continue.

After commenting, summarize the same state to the master and explicitly request publication approval.

## 6. Approval gate

Wait for an explicit approval from the master to publish.

Approval must clearly authorize creating the issue branch and pull request for this completed work. Silence, issue assignment, a Linear status change, an earlier request to implement, or approval from another agent does not satisfy this gate.

If the master requests changes instead:

1. Apply and verify them.
2. Add a delta-only follow-up comment when the changes are material, covering only the new fixes, decisions, and verification. Otherwise update the canonical comment.
3. Request approval again.

## 7. Create the issue branch and pull request

Only after explicit approval:

1. Re-read the Linear issue and its newest comments for late changes.
2. Recheck repository status and confirm the repository default branch.
3. Confirm the local change set contains only work for this issue.
4. Create a new branch whose name is exactly the Linear issue identifier, for example `SKI-123`. Do not add a prefix or description.
5. If that exact branch already exists locally or remotely, inspect it and ask the master before reusing, overwriting, renaming, or force-pushing it.
6. Stage only issue-scoped files.
7. Create an intentional commit referencing the Linear issue identifier.
8. Push the new branch without force.
9. Create a pull request into the repository's confirmed default branch.
10. Include the Linear issue link, implementation summary, verification results, rollout notes, and known limitations in the pull-request body.
11. Never merge the pull request unless the master separately requests it.

After the pull request is created, update the canonical completion comment with a Publication subsection containing the branch name, commit, pull-request link, target branch, any verification performed since the previous update, and remaining review or rollout requirements.

Do not create a second completion-style comment merely because the work moved from local completion to a branch or pull request. If the canonical comment cannot be updated, post a short publication-only follow-up containing only the new publication information.

## Failure rules

- Never invent issue details, repository identity, branch names, test results, comments, approvals, or pull-request URLs.
- Never mark the Linear issue done or change its status unless the master explicitly requests that state change.
- Never use destructive Git operations or force push.
- If Linear or repository tools are unavailable, report the missing capability and stop at the affected step.
- Before writing a comment, skip or update any existing comment that already communicates the same state for the same work revision.
- If publication partially succeeds, report exact external state and resume from that state; do not duplicate comments, branches, commits, or pull requests.

Treat the master as the user or orchestrating agent that supplied the Linear issue and controls publication approval.

## Preconditions

- Require an exact Linear issue identifier or URL from the master.
- Require access to the Linear workspace and the relevant repository.
- If the issue, repository, or authorization cannot be resolved exactly, stop and ask the master. Never guess.
- Do not create a branch, commit, push, or pull request before the approval gate below.

## 1. Read the complete Linear record

Use the connected Linear tools as the authoritative issue source.

1. Retrieve the issue by its exact identifier with relations and releases when supported.
2. Read the full description, acceptance criteria, status, priority, labels, assignee, project, cycle, parent, sub-issues, blockers, blocked items, related issues, releases, links, and attachments.
3. Read every issue comment and continue through pagination until complete.
4. Follow linked Linear documents or projects when they contain requirements needed to execute the issue.
5. Inspect embedded images or attachments when they may contain requirements or reproduction evidence.
6. Distinguish explicit requirements from discussion, inference, and superseded guidance. Prefer the newest explicit decision when comments revise the description.
7. Record the issue identifier exactly as Linear displays it; this exact value will become the branch name after approval.

Do not begin implementation from a search snippet, truncated summary, issue title alone, or second-hand paraphrase.

## 2. Establish repository scope

- Resolve the target repository and its default branch from the issue, repository metadata, linked pull requests, or the master.
- Inspect repository instructions, contribution rules, relevant specifications, tests, and surrounding implementation before editing.
- Inspect Git status first. Preserve all pre-existing changes and never include unrelated work.
- If the checkout has overlapping user changes, is based on an ambiguous branch, or does not match the issue's repository, stop and ask the master before modifying it.
- Do not fetch, switch branches, rewrite history, discard changes, or publish anything merely to resolve ambiguity.

## 3. Clarify only when needed

After reading the entire issue and inspecting the relevant code, identify missing decisions that would materially change the implementation, acceptance criteria, security, data handling, compatibility, deployment behavior, or public API.

- Ask the master concise, specific questions for blocking ambiguities.
- Explain the competing interpretations and their impact.
- Pause until answered when a reasonable assumption could produce the wrong product behavior or an unsafe change.
- If no blocking ambiguity remains, state any low-risk assumptions and continue without asking ceremonial questions.
- Treat answers from the master as additions to the issue requirements. Re-read the issue if the master says it was updated.

## 4. Implement and verify locally

- Implement only the issue scope, including required tests, documentation, migrations, or generated artifacts.
- Follow repository-native patterns and use the narrowest non-regressive change.
- Preserve unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked files.
- Validate in proportion to risk. Run focused tests first, then the broader required gates.
- Diagnose failures and distinguish issue-caused failures from pre-existing or environmental failures.
- Do not claim completion while acceptance criteria remain unverified.
- Do not create a branch, commit, push, pull request, release, or deployment during this stage unless the master separately expands the scope.

## Linear comment hygiene

Before creating or updating a Linear comment, re-read the issue's existing comments and locate the latest comment created by this agent for the current work cycle.

- Maintain one canonical completion and publication comment.
- Retain the canonical comment ID so the same comment can be updated after publication.
- Treat a proposed comment as a near duplicate when it repeats the same implementation summary, design decisions, verification results, and risks while only adding branch, commit, push, or pull-request metadata.
- Update the canonical comment instead of creating a near duplicate.
- Skip the write entirely when it adds no new information.
- Add a follow-up comment only for a material delta, such as changed requirements, additional fixes, new verification results, a blocker or its resolution, or a new rollout or review decision.
- Keep follow-up comments delta-only. Do not repeat unchanged implementation and verification summaries.
- If comment updates are unavailable, post a short delta-only follow-up rather than another completion-style summary.

## 5. Report completion on Linear

When the implementation and local verification are complete, create or update one canonical comment on the original Linear issue containing:

- What was implemented.
- Important behavior or design decisions.
- Files or system areas changed.
- Tests and checks run, with pass/fail counts where available.
- Any verification that could not be run and the exact reason.
- Remaining risks, follow-ups, migrations, or rollout requirements.
- A clear statement that the work is local and awaiting the master's approval for branch and pull-request publication.

If this agent already posted a canonical completion comment for the current work cycle, update that comment rather than creating another. Retain the returned comment ID for the publication update.

Do not post a completion comment if required work is still incomplete. Post a blocker update instead when progress cannot continue.

After commenting, summarize the same state to the master and explicitly request publication approval.

## 6. Approval gate

Wait for an explicit approval from the master to publish.

Approval must clearly authorize creating the issue branch and pull request for this completed work. Silence, issue assignment, a Linear status change, an earlier request to implement, or approval from another agent does not satisfy this gate.

If the master requests changes instead:

1. Apply and verify them.
2. Add a delta-only follow-up comment when the changes are material, covering only the new fixes, decisions, and verification. Otherwise update the canonical comment.
3. Request approval again.

## 7. Create the issue branch and pull request

Only after explicit approval:

1. Re-read the Linear issue and its newest comments for late changes.
2. Recheck repository status and confirm the repository default branch.
3. Confirm the local change set contains only work for this issue.
4. Create a new branch whose name is exactly the Linear issue identifier, for example `SKI-123`. Do not add a prefix or description.
5. If that exact branch already exists locally or remotely, inspect it and ask the master before reusing, overwriting, renaming, or force-pushing it.
6. Stage only issue-scoped files.
7. Create an intentional commit referencing the Linear issue identifier.
8. Push the new branch without force.
9. Create a pull request into the repository's confirmed default branch.
10. Include the Linear issue link, implementation summary, verification results, rollout notes, and known limitations in the pull-request body.
11. Never merge the pull request unless the master separately requests it.

After the pull request is created, update the canonical completion comment with a Publication subsection containing the branch name, commit, pull-request link, target branch, any verification performed since the previous update, and remaining review or rollout requirements.

Do not create a second completion-style comment merely because the work moved from local completion to a branch or pull request. If the canonical comment cannot be updated, post a short publication-only follow-up containing only the new publication information.

## Failure rules

- Never invent issue details, repository identity, branch names, test results, comments, approvals, or pull-request URLs.
- Never mark the Linear issue done or change its status unless the master explicitly requests that state change.
- Never use destructive Git operations or force push.
- If Linear or repository tools are unavailable, report the missing capability and stop at the affected step.
- Before writing a comment, skip or update any existing comment that already communicates the same state for the same work revision.
- If publication partially succeeds, report exact external state and resume from that state; do not duplicate comments, branches, commits, or pull requests.

"},{"type":"input_text","text":"{"dataIssue":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\"id\":\"DATA-1\",\"title\":\"Add tenant placement and canonical-gateway routing to DataFn multi-region\",\"description\":\"## Executive summary\\n\\nExtend DataFn's existing multi-region support from a global permission-grant directory into a complete, tenant-aware regional routing contract. Applications should be able to expose one stable DataFn endpoint while a trusted gateway resolves a namespace/tenant to its owning regional cell and dispatches the request server-side.\\n\\nThe core contract must remain provider-neutral and must not require clients to resolve regional hostnames.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `datafn/server/src/plugins/multi-region.ts` defines `datafnMultiRegionPlugin({ regionId, directory })`, but the directory currently indexes permission grants only.\\n* The existing index records `resourceRegion` and supports principal/resource queries through `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter`.\\n* Permission-directory writes already use a durable post-commit outbox/retry path under `datafn/server/src/execution/mutation/permission-directory-outbox.ts`.\\n* `datafn/server/src/server.ts` builds one server around one database adapter. Request context and `namespaceProvider` select a namespace, but no first-class hook validates that the namespace belongs to the current regional database or dispatches to another server.\\n* `datafn/core/src/types.ts` exposes query/search/mutation/sync hooks, but no region-placement, pre-execution routing, or transport-forwarding contract.\\n* `datafn/client/src/transport/http.ts` uses a fixed base URL and only retries authorization failures; `datafn/client/src/client.ts` accepts a fixed `remote` or custom `remoteAdapter`.\\n* `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter` offers indexed reads and `putIfAbsent`, but `update` is not compare-and-set; `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter` separately exposes optional `compareAndSet`.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nDataFn can tell consumers that a shared resource grant originated in a region, but it cannot authoritatively place a tenant namespace, reject execution in the wrong regional database, or let a global gateway forward a request safely. Applications would otherwise need to build their own router around DataFn and teach clients about regional endpoints, fragmenting behavior across consumers.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Make tenant/namespace placement a first-class DataFn multi-region capability.\\n* Support a canonical gateway URL with no regional hostname resolution in clients.\\n* Preserve current single-region and permission-directory behavior.\\n* Keep storage and transport adapters cloud/provider neutral.\\n* Guarantee that wrong-region detection happens before reads/writes are executed.\\n* Cover HTTP query/mutation/search, sync/push/pull/reconcile, in-process execution, and WebSocket lifecycle.\\n* Define safe placement changes without claiming transparent active-active writes.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Distinguish placement from permission indexing\\n\\nExtend or compose `datafnMultiRegionPlugin` with an authoritative placement directory. A placement record should include at least:\\n\\n* stable tenant/namespace ID;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* monotonically changing routing epoch/version;\\n* lifecycle state (`active`, `moving`, `tombstoned`);\\n* updated timestamp and optional cache expiry;\\n* adapter-owned internal destination reference, separate from a public URL.\\n\\nPermission-grant indexing may reference placement, but it must not become the source of truth for namespace ownership. Document separate consistency and recovery guarantees for both directories.\\n\\n### 2. Define provider-neutral directory capabilities\\n\\nSpecify the atomic contract needed for initial `putIfAbsent` placement and controlled compare-and-set moves. Decide whether to extend `IndexedDirectoryStoreAdapter`, compose it with `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, or introduce a focused `DatafnPlacementDirectoryAdapter`.\\n\\nCore must run against in-memory/test adapters. Provider integrations may implement DynamoDB Global Tables, Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or other stores.\\n\\n### 3. Add pre-execution placement validation\\n\\nResolve the trusted namespace after authentication/context construction and before authorization side effects, database queries, mutations, sync changes, or plugin hooks that assume local ownership.\\n\\nIf the current server does not own the namespace/epoch, return a typed internal `DATAFN_REGION_MISMATCH`/moving response containing safe routing metadata. Do not trust a raw client-supplied namespace or region header without existing authentication and namespace authorization.\\n\\nThis validation must also cover in-process executor requests and custom server routes that operate on regional data.\\n\\n### 4. Add a gateway dispatcher/transport contract\\n\\nProvide an adapter boundary that lets a canonical ingress:\\n\\n1. authenticate enough context to derive the tenant/namespace;\\n2. resolve placement;\\n3. forward internally to the owning cell;\\n4. attach a short-lived signed routing assertion;\\n5. retry one time after a pre-execution stale-epoch response.\\n\\nThe internal destination may be a service binding, HTTP origin, RPC stub, or function reference. DataFn core must not depend on Cloudflare, AWS, DNS, or public regional URLs.\\n\\n### 5. Preserve request semantics and idempotency\\n\\nForward method, path, body, auth context, request/correlation ID, namespace, and idempotency identity without allowing callers to forge gateway headers. Define bounded retry rules for:\\n\\n* query/search/status;\\n* mutation/transact;\\n* push/pull/reconcile/seed/clone;\\n* public-link and permission-grant operations;\\n* custom plugin routes.\\n\\nMutating replay is allowed only when DataFn can prove the original request did not begin execution or when the operation's existing idempotency key makes replay safe.\\n\\n### 6. Define WebSocket and sync behavior\\n\\nA WebSocket/sync session is routed during handshake and pinned to namespace + region + routing epoch. When placement changes, the old cell must stop accepting new work and cause clients to reconnect through the canonical gateway. Ordering, cursor semantics, mutation IDs, and pull checkpoints must remain valid or fail explicitly across migration.\\n\\nThe browser/client API should continue to accept one stable `remote`/`wsUrl` in gateway mode. Direct regional routing can remain an opt-in adapter mode.\\n\\n### 7. Placement migration protocol\\n\\nDocument and implement a minimal safe state machine, including:\\n\\n* quiesce/fence source writes;\\n* drain/reconcile outbox work;\\n* copy and validate tenant data;\\n* atomically advance the placement epoch;\\n* warm/route target reads;\\n* resume writes;\\n* retain rollback/tombstone evidence.\\n\\nNo request may write to both cells because of stale cache state. State transitions and failure recovery must be observable and testable.\\n\\n### 8. Observability and compatibility\\n\\nEmit safe events/metrics for placement lookup, cache hit, forward, mismatch, retry, moving, directory unavailable, destination unavailable, and epoch conflict. Existing single-region configurations and the current permission-directory API must remain source-compatible.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n- [ ] A DataFn client configured with one canonical HTTP endpoint can query and mutate namespaces owned by at least two regional database adapters without learning regional hostnames.\\n- [ ] Current single-region servers and permission-directory grant indexing continue to pass their existing tests.\\n- [ ] Every built-in HTTP, sync, in-process, and WebSocket entry path validates placement before regional database execution.\\n- [ ] A caller cannot route into or select another tenant by spoofing namespace, region, epoch, or internal-forwarding headers.\\n- [ ] Initial placement is atomic, and placement moves use a fenced compare-and-set epoch transition.\\n- [ ] Stale gateway cache causes at most one bounded re-resolution/retry and no duplicate mutation side effects.\\n- [ ] WebSocket clients reconnect through the canonical gateway on a move, with explicit cursor/checkpoint behavior.\\n- [ ] Permission-directory outbox behavior is reconciled with placement moves; failed indexing does not silently change ownership.\\n- [ ] Directory and target-cell outages return documented retryability and do not route to a random/default region.\\n- [ ] Core conformance tests run with in-memory adapters, and at least two provider adapters demonstrate portability.\\n- [ ] Public API/type documentation explains gateway mode, direct mode, consistency, migration, and operational requirements.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n\\n* Implementing a Skillplane-specific workspace directory.\\n* Requiring active-active writes for the same namespace.\\n* Choosing a cloud provider, global database, DNS layout, or edge platform.\\n* Automatically In gateway mode, browsers, mobile clients, and MCP/OAuth clients continue to use the canonical hostname; regional authorities remain an optional direct-routing deployment mode, not a client requirement.\\n\\nThe implementation must remain provider-neutral. A consumer may back the global identity-to-region directory with DynamoDB Global Tables, Cloudflare Durable Objects, Redis, PostgreSQL, or another adapter that satisfies AuthFn's consistency contract.\\n\\n## Current implementation basis\\n\\nVerified against current `sf-next/next` head `523c66ae8cf981ff8331d56386cec1f81c704182`:\\n\\n* `authfn/multi-region/src/index.ts` registers `beforeUserCreate`, `afterUserCreate`, `beforeSessionIssue`, and `afterAccountDelete` hooks and exposes `POST /regions/lookup` plus `GET /environment`.\\n* `authfn/core/src/core/regions.ts` resolves the current region primarily from request host/authority, performs lookup/registration through `ConditionalKVStoreAdapter`, and raises `AuthFnRegionMismatchError` for the client to follow.\\n* `authfn/client/src/regional-client.ts` keeps a local identifier-to-region cache and requires `resolveBaseUrl(regionId)`; routing retries therefore live in every client.\\n* `authfn/core/src/plugin-types.ts` already defines region, lookup, registration, and runtime configuration contracts.\\n* `packages/db/src/adapter/types.ts` provides atomic `setIfAbsent` and optional `compareAndSet`.\\n* Python's `authfn/plugins/multi_region.py` uses a separate duck-typed `directory.lookup_by_identifier/register_user` contract and does not currently expose the same atomic ownership semantics as TypeScript.\\n\\n## Problem\\n\\nThe existing model assumes the caller can discover a user's region, map a region ID to a public hostname, and retry against that hostname. That complicates every client and OAuth callback, exposes deployment topology, and makes canonical issuer/cookie behavior harder to reason about.\\n\\nMoving this logic to a gateway creates a shared dependency: if the global ingress or directory cannot route a request, otherwise healthy regional authentication cells may be unreachable through the canonical authority. The contract must therefore define availability, caching, consistency, and failure behavior explicitly rather than hiding them inside one provider integration.\\n\\n## Goals\\n\\n* Add a gateway-routed mode while preserving the current direct regional-authority mode.\\n* Keep one stable public issuer/base URL for browser auth, OAuth discovery/callbacks, MCP authorization, and native handoff flows.\\n* Make regional lookup and dispatch a server-side concern; clients do not need regional DNS names or `resolveBaseUrl` in gateway mode.\\n* Keep lookup storage and inter-region transport provider-neutral.\\n* Preserve atomic, deterministic account placement under concurrent sign-up.\\n* Avoid turning the public lookup endpoint into an account-enumeration or topology-disclosure surface.\\n* Bring TypeScript and Python behavior and interfaces into parity.\\n\\n## Required design\\n\\n### 1. Separate public authority from execution region\\n\\nIntroduce explicit concepts for:\\n\\n* canonical public authority/issuer;\\n* current execution `regionId`;\\n* internal regional destination;\\n* routing mode (`direct` or `gateway`);\\n* routing version/epoch used to reject stale decisions.\\n\\nHost matching may remain for direct mode, but gateway mode must not infer ownership from the public host because every request arrives on the same hostname.\\n\\n### 2. Define a gateway-facing routing contract\\n\\nProvide a framework-owned contract that a gateway can call before invoking AuthFn, for example a resolver/dispatcher result containing:\\n\\n* normalized lookup key or opaque routing subject;\\n* owning `regionId`;\\n* routing epoch/version;\\n* decision status (`local`, `forward`, `unknown`, `moving`, `unavailable`);\\n* an internal destination token or adapter-owned handle, not necessarily a public URL;\\n* cacheability/expiry metadata.\\n\\nDo not require Cloudflare Service Bindings, DynamoDB, or any specific transport in the core API. Provider packages may adapt the contract.\\n\\n### 3. Keep placement atomic\\n\\nContinue to use `setIfAbsent` for first ownership and use `compareAndSet` (or an equivalent required capability) for controlled moves. Specify normalized identifier keys, conflict handling, deletion/tombstone behavior, read consistency, and replication-lag expectations.\\n\\nAn account must never be created in two regions when concurrent requests race. Registration rollback and retry behavior must be tested under partial failure.\\n\\n### 4. Add trusted internal forwarding\\n\\nDefine a short-lived signed internal routing assertion containing at least request ID, target region, routing epoch, issued/expiry timestamps, and a replay-resistant nonce or equivalent transport protection. Regional handlers must reject user-supplied forwarding headers and validate the assertion before trusting gateway routing context.\\n\\nForwarding must preserve method, path, body, cookies, CSRF properties, client IP provenance policy, and request correlation without leaking internal destinations to callers.\\n\\n### 5. Make retries side-effect safe\\n\\nA regional instance must validate placement before creating users, issuing sessions/codes/tokens, sending OTP email, or performing any other externally visible effect. If the decision is stale, return a machine-readable internal mismatch response and let the gateway re-resolve and retry at most once.\\n\\nDo not automatically replay requests after a side effect may have occurred. Define idempotency requirements for OTP send, OAuth authorization/token exchange, account creation, API-key operations, password reset, email change, native handoff, and deletion.\\n\\n### 6. Preserve canonical OAuth/session semantics\\n\\nIn gateway mode:\\n\\n* OAuth metadata, authorization endpoint, token endpoint, redirect URIs, and issuer remain canonical.\\n* OAuth state/authorization requests/codes and native handoff artifacts carry enough region/epoch context to return to the correct cell without changing the browser-visible host.\\n* Cookies retain one documented domain/name/security policy across regions.\\n* Sessions expose region metadata only where useful and do not require a regional public origin.\\n* Logout, revocation, refresh rotation, account deletion, and session invalidation work across the canonical authority.\\n\\n### 7. Harden public behavior\\n\\nThe public API must not reveal whether an identifier exists, its user ID, its region, or internal authority unless a consumer explicitly opts into the legacy/direct lookup behavior and accepts that security posture. Gateway lookup should be an authenticated internal capability.\\n\\nUpdate event/metric schemas to distinguish lookup hit/miss/conflict, forwarding, stale epoch, retry, directory unavailable, and target unavailable without logging raw identifiers.\\n\\n### 8. TypeScript/Python parity and compatibility\\n\\nDefine one documented semantic contract across both SDKs. Existing direct-mode configuration and regional client behavior remain backward compatible. Add migration notes for consumers moving from public regional authorities to a canonical gateway.\\n\\n## Acceptance criteria\\n\\n- [ ] A client configured only with a canonical AuthFn base URL can complete OTP sign-up/sign-in, cookie sessions, OAuth authorization-code + refresh, API-key auth, logout/revocation, and native handoff for users owned by at least two regions.\\n- [ ] The gateway resolves and forwards without returning a regional hostname to the client.\\n- [ ] Direct regional-authority mode and existing `resolveBaseUrl` clients continue to work.\\n- [ ] Concurrent first sign-up claims cannot create the same normalized identifier in two regions.\\n- [ ] Stale routing produces a pre-side-effect mismatch, one bounded gateway re-resolution, and no duplicate email/session/code/token side effects.\\n- [ ] Missing directory or target-cell availability fails with explicit retryable/non-retryable errors and documented cache/fail-closed behavior.\\n- [ ] User-controlled headers cannot spoof region, epoch, or internal forwarding identity.\\n- [ ] Public responses do not disclose account existence or regional topology in gateway mode.\\n- [ ] OAuth issuer/resource discovery and callback URLs remain canonical throughout the flow.\\n- [ ] TypeScript and Python conformance suites cover equivalent lookup, claim, mismatch, routing, and failure semantics.\\n- [ ] Core tests use in-memory adapters; at least two provider adapters demonstrate the same conformance contract without becoming core dependencies.\\n- [ ] Architecture and migration documentation explain the global dependency and operational SLOs.\\n\\n## Non-goals\\n\\n* Building Skillplane's deployment topology in AuthFn.\\n* Mandating active-active writes for one account.\\n* Requiring a particular cloud, DNS provider, global database, or service-binding product.\\n* Silently failing over an account to another region without an explicit migration
